    Yes, My Toddler Sleeps In Our Room. No, We Haven't Stopped Having Sex.

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Before you judge me, I asked experts what young kids actually understand and if our obsession with sexual privacy is more cultural and modern than we think.
    • My 3-year-old still sleeps in bed with my husband and me.
    • To which I say: We manage just fine, thanks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Before you judge me, I asked experts what young kids actually understand and if our obsession with sexual privacy is more cultural and modern than we think.

    My 3-year-old still sleeps in bed with my husband and me. I like cuddling him all night, and I’ve come to accept that it’s just the kind of mom I am: the clingy co-sleeping type. When he was littler, we took safe-sleep precautions with a bassinet and all that jazz, but these days, he sleeps right up next to me. Most non-co-sleeping families cringe at this. And then they immediately want to know: So how do you get intimate with your partner?

    To which I say: We manage just fine, thanks. But lately, I’ve been wondering about the elephant in the room. Or, should I say, the toddler.

    In a recent development, my husband and I NEVER have sex in the bed with our toddler. But we do sneak into the bathroom. Or sometimes, once he’s deeply asleep, we pull out a cot on the other side of the room and get it on in the dark. I’m embarrassed even admitting that.

    I also don’t believe we’re the only parents who have ever found themselves in this predicament.

    It has been revealed that here’s the thing... our house isn’t huge. And between the 3-year-old sleeping soundly in our blacked-out bedroom and one of our much more aware older kids wandering out of their rooms, we’ve chosen the former.

    Which brings me to something else we really need to address. What about the “olden days”? Ma and Pa from Little House on the Prairie managed to have four babies while living in one-room log cabins and shanties. I guarantee they weren’t heading out to the barn or the outhouse every time they wanted to have sex, especially when bears and wolves were roaming around, and temperatures dipped below zero.

    Besides, many modern families around the world still live and sleep in shared spaces.

    It has been revealed that lately I’ve wondered if being horrified by the idea of parents having sex in the same room as a sleeping child is a cultural thing. Is it so awful if they’re still very little? At what point does “they have no idea what’s happening” turn into “Mom and Dad need to find somewhere else to do this”?

    We reached out to experts to answer all the questions you’ve probably been dying to know but have been way too embarrassed to ask.

    It has been revealed that here’s the short answer: Parents don’t need to feel guilty about having sex in the same room as a newborn or young infant. An infant doesn’t have the “cognitive capacity to understand what sex is,” and they won’t remember or understand what’s going on, notes Kimberly Resnick Anderson, LCSW, an AASECT-certified sex therapist.

    Anderson does add one caveat, though. Having a baby nearby is likely to make parents more reserved and overall less expressive during sex. Over time, she notes, that could potentially lead to a “more permanent shift” in how they express themselves sexually.

    Industry observers note that when does she recommend finding some privacy? Around age 1.

    Once a child develops language and becomes mobile, she notes, it becomes harder to get it on, knowing the child could wake up in the middle of it.

    In a recent development, but Samantha Ridout, M.Phil., BCBA, a child development and behavioral expert, cautions against treating any birthday as a universal cutoff. No two children develop at exactly the same rate, she says, so there isn’t a magical age when a child suddenly becomes aware of what’s happening around them. Instead, parents should watch for their child’s growing alertness and awareness and set appropriate boundaries.

    I’ve found this to be true in my own family. We moved our older two kids out of our room quicker because they were definitely more aware than our last, who just feels more “babyish.”.

    But both experts made one thing very clear: During sex, infants need to be in a separate, safe sleep space.

    Let’s go back to my Ma and Pa observation for a minute, shall we?

    It has been revealed that the idea of children and adults having separate bedrooms is a relatively upcoming phenomenon, states Macall Gordon, a researcher and sleep coach with an undergraduate degree in anthropology who studies children’s sleep through a sociohistorical lens. She says before the lightbulb was invented, family life revolved around sunrise and sunset, with families often sleeping in shared spaces.

    It has been revealed that but with electricity, adults could suddenly stay up after children went to bed, she adds. Now, children needed a “separate space to sleep” while adults stayed up. So the nursery and the crib came along. Then, she indicates, the layout of homes started to change, too, to include hallways connecting separate rooms. Before that, rooms were all connected to each other, so you had to go through one to get to another.

    According to recent reports, to this day, however, a separate bedroom is still something of a privilege. Many families simply don’t have “extra, separate rooms,” Gordon points out, especially in substantial cities, where studios and lofts are common, or in cultures where extended family members may occupy additional bedrooms. “While we think of a separate room for children as the norm, it really wasn’t for most of our history,” Gordon shares.

    Tiffany Belanger, cosleeping expert and founder of Cosleepy, says the topic tends to divide her followers into two camps: those who will have sex in the room with a kid and those who won’t. When I described my scenario to her, she responded that floor sex while young kids are still sleeping in their parents’ bed is actually pretty common among the co-sleeping families she hears from.

    You want to know if mine has woken up before.

    In a recent development, but rarely. He’s a really deep sleeper, and it’s only happened a few times. It’s dark, and when he did wake up, he immediately called out for me in that disoriented, half-asleep way toddlers do. We stopped immediately. The cot is also on the far side of the bed, outside his line of sight. As far as I know, he never saw or heard anything.

    It has been revealed that will we emotionally damage our kid if he were to catch us in the act? Unlikely, Ridout says, if parents stay calm, stop immediately, tell the child they are safe, and answer their questions in a simple, non-panicky way.

    But all of this still leaves me with the extremely practical question that got us into this mess in the first place.

    Parents have to get creative, flexible, and spontaneous, says Anderson. That might mean asking family or friends to babysit when you can, doing it in other rooms, or using whatever short pockets of privacy you can find.

    And while Belanger reassures me that my floor-sex solution isn't unheard of among co-sleeping parents, the other experts think it’s not a great option when kids become mobile and verbal. So, I suppose it might be time to retire the cot. Where to next?

    Latest Update: This ‘unhinged’ advice for toddler moms is actually pretty genius

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that toddlers are a wild ride. They’re old enough to have opinions, verbal enough to pepper in words like “actually” and small enough to go fully boneless in the cereal aisle when overruled. But with the right frame of mind and a little patience, we can outsmart them.

    A recent Threads post from @jayonathequeen asked parents for their best “unhinged advice” for raising toddlers, and the replies poured in. Some came from toddler room teachers, longtime nannies and even doctors. Most came from moms who’ve logged countless hours negotiating with toddlers and consulting their pediatricians. We’ve all earned our stripes, and sometimes there’s nothing like raw mom-to-mom advice.

    Many of the suggestions are surprisingly hinged. And certainly no one’s judging.

    Anyone who has turned around in a parking lot to find an empty space where a small person used to be knows this particular brand of panic. The thread’s most-liked reply, with nearly 18,000 hearts, went straight at the escape artist problem, and the moms underneath it kept the ideas coming.

    Credit: @thriving_out_of_spite, @norcalcaro and @sksargeant via Threads.

    One mom’s solution doubled as entertainment.

    Credit: @champersstamers via Threads.

    (If you try this one, stick with a foil balloon, since popped latex is a choking hazard for little kids.).

    According to recent reports, toddler palates are a moving target. The food they inhaled one day is suddenly disgusting the next. A couple of moms found that a little creative branding goes a long way, at the table and beyond.

    Credit: @analee_inreallife via Threads.

    Recent findings suggest that brushing teeth, putting on shoes, surviving the checkout aisle. The daily stuff is where most battles originate, and, in turn, where moms get the most inventive. A common thread here is giving toddlers a sense of control while you cleverly steer the ship.

    Credit: @parentnest.digital via Threads.

    Credit: @suziespree via Threads.

    And sometimes the smartest move is picking your battles.

    Credit: @cryssinikki via Threads.

    When a meltdown hits, plenty of moms agreed the first move is regulating yourself. Toddlers take their emotional cues from us, so the calmer we stay, the faster they come back down.

    Credit: @sin_standard via Threads.

    From there, a little misdirection can work wonders.

    Credit: @thenerdyderma via Threads.

    Credit: @josephineadel via Threads.

    In a recent development, that sniff trick is a cousin of the viral “Jessica” trick, where a parent interrupts a meltdown by calmly calling for someone who isn’t there. Pediatrician Dr. Madison Szar told Motherly that “What’s that smell?” works just as well, since the surprise is what breaks the loop. Bonus points for the deep breaths.

    And for the moments when you’re the one about to lose it, one mom has a suggestion that sounds unhinged until you hear her out.

    Credit: @kaitlyn_e.a via Threads.

    Then there are the white lies. One bedtime fib stood out as particularly clever.

    Credit: @kellywills901 via Threads.

    Sources indicate that having raised two kids, one in college and one in high school, I can attest that I lied to them. A lot. The car won’t start unless you’re buckled. It’s against the law to take your shoes off in the store. The toy store is closing, so we have to leave now. I promise you they are both 100% trustworthy, honest people.

    When I was a new mom, just 21 and wildly out of my depth, I had a mentor with a toddler of her own. A yoga teacher who became a mom in her early 40s, she was a free spirit who didn’t mother through the lens of anyone else’s scrutiny. It was wild and refreshing.

    Industry observers note that she was willing to be inconvenienced so her son could explore and held firm when exploring teetered toward danger. She also leaned into the absurdity. At one point she’d somehow acquired a shopping cart, and when her son got grumpy, she’d load him in with a rug, some toys and their cat (I’m not kidding) and march around the neighborhood with the dog following behind.

    Sources indicate that toddlers are ridiculous, and we all know it. Sometimes you have to meet the moment with the same.

    #21645. How To Make Fewer Grocery Trips & Still Eat Well

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1352 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

    How To Make Fewer Grocery Trips & Still Eat Well

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1352 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that groceries cost a fortune, gas isn’t cheap… every “quick” run to the store somehow costs you 60 bucks or more.
    • It’s a phenomenon that happens more often than not these days: You run into the store for milk, cheese, eggs, and a few other basics, and walk out wondering how in the hell a small handful of grocery bags just set you back upwards of 100 bucks.
    • The reality is groceries are still painfully expensive, and plenty of families are stretched thinner than ever.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that groceries cost a fortune, gas isn’t cheap… every “quick” run to the store somehow costs you 60 bucks or more. Experts share how to shop less and still feed your family well.

    It’s a phenomenon that happens more often than not these days: You run into the store for milk, cheese, eggs, and a few other basics, and walk out wondering how in the hell a small handful of grocery bags just set you back upwards of 100 bucks. Worse, you then have to play budget Tetris, moving money around to make sure you have funds for the inevitable grocery run you’ll have to make next week. Add in the gas it takes to get to and from, and you’re spent literally and figuratively.

    The reality is groceries are still painfully expensive, and plenty of families are stretched thinner than ever. And, sure, cutting back on trips is probably one of the easiest and most logical ways to save money (and time, and sanity). But it begs the question: How long can you go between grocery runs without your family surviving on cereal benders?

    We asked food and budgeting experts how they personally make it work.

    Most of the experts we polled remarked one substantial shop a week is sort of the sweet spot. “Every extra trip not only takes up valuable time, but is also another chance to grab things that aren’t on the list and drive up your overall grocery bill,” says Laurie Hise, CEO of Passionate Penny Pincher.

    It has been revealed that is it possible to stretch it to every two weeks? Maybe. But AJ Prasaguet, head of the iconic Palace bar and restaurant in Miami Beach, points out that biweekly shopping “can work if you have the storage space, freezer capacity, and money available upfront. Those are real considerations, and not every household has all three.”.

    Amber Hanson, a licensed nutritionist and founder of Whole You Nutrition, emphasizes that there’s no cut-and-dry, one-size-fits-all answer. Your ideal grocery-shopping cadence will ultimately depend on things like how close you live to a store and when your paycheck hits the bank. If you get paid every two weeks, it might make sense to shop on that timeframe too.

    According to recent reports, before you make your little grocery list and head to the store, open up your own fridge, freezer, and pantry. “The best way to save money is to use what you have already paid for,” notes Hanson.

    Recent findings suggest that jenn Lueke, Latest York Times-bestselling author of Don’t Think About Dinner, does her inventory every Friday night, then builds the next week’s meals around what’s left. Example: “If I know I have a half carton of broth that needs to be used, I’ll make sure to pick up a grain, like rice or quinoa, that I can cook in it.”.

    Prasaguet goes one step further. “Give an ingredient its next job before you buy it. If a recipe needs half a container of something, decide where the other half is going.” Take cabbage, for instance. It can be slaw one night, stir-fry the next, and soup filler after that.

    According to recent reports, another tip Hise is a fan of is ordering online for pickup or delivery when you can. The simple act of skipping the aisles means you don't have to worry about impulse buys wreaking havoc on your total.

    Sources indicate that as a busy working mom who regularly feels she has to have everything for the week figured out at all times, this was very liberating to hear! As the experts remind us, life happens. Plans change. A rigid seven-night menu is a fast track to wasted food.

    But if it makes you feel better to have the week mostly lined up, you could follow Hise’s example: blueprint five “fresh” dinners a week, leaving one night for leftovers and one for a meal pulled from what’s already in the pantry, fridge, or freezer. Prasaguet relies on a similar formula: four planned dinners, one leftovers meal, one pantry or freezer dinner, on flex night. “That gives the week some structure without pretending everything will go according to plan,” he says.

    Lueke recommends starting with dinners, then exploring how you can make the most of them. “Will the slow-cooker chicken stretch to cover lunches for half the week too? Can I make a double batch of quinoa and bulk up our mid-week sheet pan dinner?” Theme nights like Taco Tuesday or Breakfast for Dinner also help reduce decision fatigue.

    The trick to making groceries last, many of the pros explained, is buying foods with different lifespans and eating them in the right order. “You do not want an entire cart of produce that all needs attention at once,” emphasizes Prasaguet.

    Lueke thinks about it in three zones:.

    According to recent reports, andrea Woroch, a consumer savings expert, notes that some hardy produce (think garlic, potatoes, sweet potatoes, winter squash, even whole apples) can last for months depending on storage conditions as well as how they’re handled. For fast-spoilers like berries, resist the urge to buy the giant fresh packs unless you know your family will gobble them down. Otherwise, stock up on frozen.

    If you're afraid frozen and canned food won't pack the same nutritional punch as fresh, well, the experts beg to differ.

    Recent findings suggest that “One of the biggest misconceptions about healthy eating is that fresh foods are always better than frozen or canned alternatives. That’s simply not the case,” indicates Jennifer Pallian, a registered dietitian and founder of Foodess. Frozen vegetables are typically flash-frozen shortly after harvest, and research has found they can be just as nutritious as fresh produce that’s been sitting in your fridge for several days. In some cases, they even have more vitamin C.”.

    It has been revealed that don’t turn your nose up at canned staples, either. Pallian is a massive proponent of canned light tuna (a solid source of protein, selenium, and omega-3s) and canned chickpeas, which pack both protein and fiber and are already cooked.

    Just opt for low-sodium or no-salt-added canned veggies and beans, and be mindful of foods packed in juices, syrups, or sauces.

    Adopting a few little habits can go a long way toward making food last until your next grocery run:.

    However, Prasaguet reminds us, “Stretching groceries should never mean stretching food safety.” That means refrigerating leftovers within two hours, eating them within three to four days, or sticking them in the freezer.

    You should know that eating well doesn’t mean you have to buy a bunch of fancy superfoods. “Some of the most nutrient-dense foods in the grocery store are also the cheapest,” Hanson says.

    Here’s what our experts say they keep stocked:.

    And while many of us think shopping in bulk must save money, Prasaguet notes that it’s “only better value if you can afford it, store it, and finish it.” Hise’s workaround is to grab a few extra cans whenever they’re on sale. “A few extra cans a month can add up to a pantry that carries you through a tight month.”.

    If you feel like a failure every time you serve your family dinner out of a bag or can, it’s high time you cut yourself some slack.

    “Frozen and canned foods that you actually eat beat fresh vegetables you throw away every time,” claims Hise. Link agrees, adding, “I’d much rather see a family use convenient foods they enjoy than buy fresh ingredients that become a science experiment in the crisper drawer.”.

    “A fed family is a win, and ‘fresh’ isn’t the measure of a good dinner," Lueke puts it simply. A balanced meal is made up of a protein, a plant or two, and something filling. It truly does not matter if those came from the produce section or the freezer aisle.

    But maybe Prasaguet sums it up best. “You do not have to prove your love through a complicated dinner,” he reassures. “Feeding your family with the resources you have is already an act of care.”.

    Latest Update: Nate Bargatze Is (Sort Of) Leading By Example

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Though he’s one of the biggest comedians in the world, Nate Bargatze’s career path was anything but straightforward.
    • It’s a bit hard to believe that Nate Bargatze, one of the biggest comedians today, met his wife while working at Applebee’s in Tennessee.
    • But authenticity matters to him, in his storytelling and what he’s learned over the years.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Though he’s one of the biggest comedians in the world, Nate Bargatze’s career path was anything but straightforward.

    It’s a bit hard to believe that Nate Bargatze, one of the biggest comedians today, met his wife while working at Applebee’s in Tennessee. Or that on his first job overseeing the dog kennel in an amusement park (apparently a thing), he let the dog out (“it was a whole thing … and that was kind of the end of the dog kennel”). Or even the basic fact that at the height of his career he decided to move back to Tennessee so that his teen daughter might have a more normal life. Bargatze’s life, like his comedic work, reads like a folksy tall tale. It draws you in with the details and lulls you with its sense of warmhearted authenticity — then lands a punchline.

    But authenticity matters to him, in his storytelling and what he’s learned over the years. He recently brought some of his experience to Ford’s Accelerate conference, where he is a spokesperson for what they’re calling the “essential economy” — of skilled technicians and tradespersons, a group that, according to economists, is in short supply and needs to grow. Bargatze is an interesting choice for this forum, a comedian with a high school degree and no formal trade skills besides those he learned onstage. He went to community college for a year and worked a variety of jobs, from waiting at Applebee’s to reading water meters. But he gets the value and opportunity in trade school. “I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools. I did not go to college ... They’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, important for just the future.”.

    Nate Bargatze poses with students at the Ford Accelerate conference, which he mc-ed.

    In a recent development, he also is thinking about this because his 14-year-old is not too far from entering the workforce. “Right now it’s like, yeah, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it. But then, as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room, so you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to [instill that urgency] as a parent. And if you don’t, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you.” Which all boils down to a most authentic parenting philosophy: “Be a good example, basically.”.

    Tell me about what you’re doing right now at this Ford Accelerate event.

    What Ford is doing with this event that we’re at right now, where they’re showing kids going into trade schools ... letting kids know that this is kind of the future, that they’re going to have jobs. And it’s like we don’t know where jobs are going with AI and all this stuff, but the trade schools… We need that. I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools.

    According to recent reports, I worked the water meters. I did not go to college. They’re going to get more college than I did. But they’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, important for just the future. I think they’re putting themselves in such a great position, probably better than they realize now, but they’re going to, I think, look back and just be like, “Man, that was such a good call.”.

    I’m wondering, since we’re talking about work, what’s the most vital thing you’ve learned about work in your life?

    I always go back to when I waited tables at one point and our manager there always talked about a sense of urgency. And that’s always stuck with me for some reason. It was just going to a table and just have a sense of urgency. It goes a long way when you get to that table and they really feel like they’re being taken care of. I think I’ve just kept that even as I’ve gone forward. If you respond to emails or my team is talking to you, I don’t want to be like, “I’ll get to them next week.” You kind of want to just be like, “No, let’s get to them and let’s make sure that we stay on top of it.”.

    Nate Bargatze plays an off-the-rails George Washington when he hosted SNL in 2024.

    Speaking of people who don’t have it, how do you instill that sense of urgency in your kid without them fighting back?

    You say stuff as a parent, you don’t know what’s sticking and what’s not sticking. You keep talking about it, and the older she gets — she’s 14 now — the more she’s going to see examples of it. Right now, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it, but then as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room. So you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to do it as a parent. And if you don’t do it, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you. And so, be a good example, basically.

    Then what’s one thing you wish your kids had today that you had during your childhood?

    Recent findings suggest that I think not the internet, maybe. That would be something, even though it’s great and the connection and it’s all this stuff, you just wish they would’ve had a little more... I think innocence lasted longer when we grew up because you just weren’t pounded with information all day long.

    What’s your wife love about you?

    I hope me for being me. We’ve been together before any of this started. We met at Applebee’s. Our 20th wedding anniversary is Oct. 13. I think it’s taking time to get used to it, but we’re along this ride together and just the surprises. We don’t know where everything’s going to end up or what’s going to happen. I think that she sees that I work hard at stuff and has been behind the scenes and loved me before any of this and loves me now. So it’s just to have the support from her, I wouldn’t be here without her. And she very much kept me grounded in a world when you come up in comedy that you could not be... It’s easy to not be grounded.

    On the flip side, what do they maybe find annoying about you?

    It has been revealed that she doesn’t like eating near me because she thinks I’d chew loud. I don’t think I’m too loud. I think it’s very normal. But she gets very uncomfortable if she’s like... I mean, if she’s on the couch and I’m at the table right behind the couch, she cannot stand it. So I eat outside now — and I only do soups.

    What kind of dad are you? How would you describe yourself as a dad?

    Recent findings suggest that I like to be... You find moments to talk to your kid. As they get older, they have friends. She’s young and all that, so they want to run with their friends. A big part is finding the moments of when they can get very talkative, and so you can find these little pockets and really try to home in on those.

    In a recent development, she knows I’m a fun time. She can take me for a ride, where her mom can put her foot down a little bit more. She knows where to go. She thinks very much like me, and she can work you if she wants something, and she works me quite a bit.

    Coming back to the work thing, what was your first job?

    Recent findings suggest that my first job, I worked at Opryland Theme Park in Nashville. I was 15, and so I was a sweeper. I walked around and just swept up the park. And I also did the dog kennel. After the sweeper, I got promoted to dog kennel.

    Nate Bargatze with his wife, Laura Bargatze.

    Well, because people would bring their pets because they’re on vacation and they’d travel with their pets.

    So you can’t bring them to the park. And so people would bring their dogs in or whatever, their cats. I think we had a chicken. People travel with some weird animals. But one dog got out, and so it was a whole thing. And that was kind of the end of the dog kennel. I think I went back to sweeping after that. But he got out, and so we had to call the... again, pre-internet, so you got to announce to the park, “Whose German shepherd got out in the parking lot?” And then they got to go search for this dog and it was under a parked car. And yeah, I still talk to that family today.

    I’m sure you don’t. They don’t want to talk to you.

    No. But I bet they still remember it. We both still remember that.

    #21643. How To Have A Lazy Thanksgiving Without Losing That Holiday Magic

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1042 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

    How To Have A Lazy Thanksgiving Without Losing That Holiday Magic

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1042 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Delegate the sides, veto the cranberry sauce, and actually sit down at your own table.
    • As a child, I remember the holiday season feeling like the most magical time of the year.
    • Who invited the guests and organized the whole Thanksgiving affair?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Delegate the sides, veto the cranberry sauce, and actually sit down at your own table.

    As a child, I remember the holiday season feeling like the most magical time of the year. Thanksgiving, in particular, seemed like a big deal because it meant Christmas was right around the corner. The house always felt so warm and cozy with fall decorations on full display — their last hurrah before Christmas took over. And the food. There was always so much delicious food to consume. It was wonderful. It was special. And now, as an adult, I realize it was all thanks to... my mom.

    Who decorated the house like that? Mom. Who invited the guests and organized the whole Thanksgiving affair? Mom. Who made all of that yummy food? You guessed it — Mom! For me, all of that stuff just seemed to magically get done without much fuss. But there was a fuss. And it wasn’t magic. It was Mom. And now that I’m a mom myself, I realize just how much she had on her plate, figuratively speaking. (Literally, she probably didn’t have much on her plate at all because she was too busy hosting to actually enjoy the meal she created.).

    Industry observers note that the point is, Thanksgiving can prove to be such a stressful time for moms with all the planning and cooking and putting everyone else’s needs above their own. So much effort is put into making this day perfect for everyone but themselves. But moms deserve to enjoy this holiday too, which is why I say it’s time to invoke a upcoming tradition known as the Lazy Thanksgiving.

    Recent findings suggest that now I know what you’re thinking, but don’t let the name fool you; a Lazy Thanksgiving doesn’t mean a Lame Thanksgiving. There are still plenty of ways to make this day feel special without completely wiping yourself out in the process. Here’s how.

    Recent findings suggest that even if you’re hosting Thanksgiving dinner, that doesn’t mean you should automatically carry the load of the entire meal on your shoulders. Do what any good boss does and delegate an assortment of dishes to other members of the family for them to bring over on the day of. If there’s one thing that you personally enjoy making, then by all means have at it. But everything else should be outsourced to others. Don’t let the burden fall solely on you.

    According to recent reports, to add a fun twist, reveal that anyone who contributes a dish gets their name entered into a raffle for a special prize at the end of the night. This could be something hassle-free and small, like a cute little ornament or a goodie bag of chocolate. This not only serves as a great incentive to help lighten your cooking load, but it also gives the winner a sweet keepsake of the occasion. (It’s worth noting that this prize part is completely optional — no family member should need to be bribed to help out.).

    Recent findings suggest that if you don’t feel comfortable with a potluck approach, but still feel overwhelmed at the thought of making so many dishes, feel free to just simply not make some of those items. (Think of it as a food-ocracy and you’re the president.) Cranberry sauce may be thought of as a Thanksgiving staple, but if only a spoonful or so gets eaten each year, then you are well within your rights to take it off the menu. The same goes for squash or yams or anything else that never ends up feeling worth the effort you put into making it. Odds are, no one is going to care or miss it, and those who do obtain the right to make it themselves.

    In a recent development, if you really want to unburden yourself and maximize your relaxation time, you could always get the food from somewhere else and either pick it up or have it delivered right to your door. Honey Baked is always a solid option with great choices for a delicious holiday feast.

    It has been revealed that it’s more expensive than making it yourself, but a lot less time-consuming, and if various family members chip in to make it happen, it could end up being more than worth the cost. That way you can sit down and actually have time to enjoy everyone’s tech giant for a change.

    Recent findings suggest that do you enjoy cooking but dread the massive clean-up job that comes at the end of it all? Trade in regular dishes and cups for paper ones. Sure, there will still be some dishes to contend with that the actual food was cooked in, but this swap definitely helps cut down on the task and leaves extra room for everything else to go in the dishwasher.

    Industry observers note that as a bonus, you can make use of all the extra paper plates by turning it into a fun craft competition for the kids. Whether they use them to make a snowman or some Thanksgiving-inspired creation, this is a great way to get their artistic juices flowing. Choose a family member to be the judge and give out a prize to the winner each year: something like a small toy or maybe even a NeeDoh if you really want the crowd to go wild and can get your hands on one. The kids will love the challenge and look forward to it as part of an annual tradition.

    According to recent reports, then again, do you want to go completely rogue? Throw tradition out the window and order takeout or make an easy casserole that will feed everyone and involve zero stress. No turkey. No stuffing. No gravy. No hassle.

    However you choose to invoke your “Lazy Thanksgiving,” just make sure that it’s the right fit for you. The whole point is to put less pressure on this day, and by extension, yourself. Remember that less work for you doesn’t equate to a less enjoyable time for everyone else. You being around more, instead of running back and forth to the kitchen, is something the whole family will be thankful for in the long run.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Give her a little something that encourages her to enjoy a few minutes of peace (and zero responsibility).

    Most of us aren’t going to turn our noses up at a pretty piece of jewelry or say no to a spa day. But if you really get to the heart of what most moms want, it’s pretty simple: to sit the f*ck down. Just for a minute. Maybe with a warm drink that we don’t have to reheat three times, maybe under a cozy blanket, definitely without someone saying “Mom? Mom? Mom” every 12 seconds (go ask your father).

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that AJ McLean, the singer, songwriter, and most tattooed member of The Backstreet Boys just moved his family to Fresh York City.

    • Industry observers note that I think I am a cool dad.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Just one of the Boys raising two girls.

    It has been revealed that AJ McLean, the singer, songwriter, and most tattooed member of The Backstreet Boys just moved his family to Fresh York City. “All three of the ladies in my life love New York,” he notes — and he’s all about it. “Celebrating Christmas in New York this year is going to be fantastic.”.

    In a recent development, but before he can take the family to the Rockettes, McLean has an album to launch (Sex, Love, and Music, out Nov. 27) and a solo tour to rock (The Better Man Tour). He is also busy as the spokesman for Delsym 12-Hour Cough Relief, which he states saved a performance during The Backstreet Boys residency at The Sphere last year. McLean took a break from his tour to take Fatherly’s Cool Dad questionnaire — and talk about staying healthy, sober, and putting family first.

    Industry observers note that I think I am a cool dad. I think I'm a cool dad because I really kind of let my kids form their own opinions and have a voice, and we work as a team. I want my girls to always have a voice. That's super vital to me. Sometimes, they have too much of a voice, but it's OK. That's when dad has to step in and reel it back a little bit. I want my girls to just always look up to their dad, and I try to set the best example that I can.

    AJ McLean on his solo “The Better Man” Tour.

    What's the best film to watch with kids?

    It has been revealed that so I'm an ’80s kid and I am so happy that I turned my girls onto Labyrinth, which they absolutely love; The Goonies, which they absolutely love; and Gremlins. They are obsessed, especially with Labyrinth. When I mentioned it to them, they were a little hesitant, and then once we watched it, I went back to work and caught wind from the wife that they've watched it repeatedly days after, and I'm like, "Yes, I did it.".

    What's one thing you wish your kids had today that you had growing up, especially as a kid from the ’80s?

    I wish they had cassette tape players. I did get a cassette tape player gift box from my boys over at Aerosmith, and it came with a cassette tape of their new album — it was a promotional thing. And I indicated it to my daughters, and they did not know what they were looking at. They put it in backwards. I'm like, "No, no, no, no, no, no." And then they were like, "What is the red button?" I said, "No, that's for recording." And they were astounded when I pressed play and this little speaker was playing and I'm like, "When your dad was growing up, that was it. That's all we had. There was no Bose surround sound, there was none of that.".

    In a recent development, and then my youngest — last year as a birthday present from one of her friends — got a Discman. And she of course put the CD in upside down, I had to show her the right way. That was painful. But she really loves her freaking Discman. She loves it. And I love that they're starting to come back where you actually have to buy the CD. I keep telling my girls, "There's pictures in there; there's thank yous; there's a whole thing. It's not just listening to the music; it's a whole package deal, where you don't get that if you're listening to iTunes. You see one picture and listen to the music, that's it. Albums were a thing." So I'm starting to get them into that now, which I really love.

    What's music have you successfully introduced your kids to?

    My oldest daughter's first album was The Beatles’ White Album. She learned every word between the ages of 2 and 3. And she was a sponge. My wife is the biggest Beatles fan out of anyone I've ever met in my life. She is diehard. So that was her first album. She's like, "This is what my kids are listening to, Beatles." I'm like, "OK.".

    AJ McLean and his family, pictured here in 2022, recently moved to New York City.

    And what music have your kids introduced you to?

    Recently, I took the family to the premiere of Michael, and my daughters knew who Michael Jackson was, but after the film, the obsession was over the top. They know songs I've never heard, deep cuts. People forget about Michael's Jackson’s Xscape album and they're saying, "Dad, play such and such a song." And I'm like, "That's not a song." They're like, "Yes, it is." They know more music, I think, now than I've ever known in my entire life. We have a very musical family, very musical family.

    What does fatherhood mean to you in the current world?

    Fatherhood, to me, means protection. It means compassion, understanding. It means listening with my ears and not my mouth, and being nonjudgmental, which I'm a very nonjudgmental person anyways, but just by nature, that's how I was raised. And trying to really broaden my daughters’ spectrum of the world, and to love everyone, and to accept everyone, and to be colorblind, to be genderblind, to be just very open and loving. And they are. They are two of the coolest kids I think any father could ever ask for. They are super smart. They are loving kids. They are people, people like me.

    They're not shy by any means. They will talk to everybody and talk their ear off, and I have no idea where they get that from. But yeah, I try to just really set an example, especially as a father and as a man, I want my daughters to look at me and then be able to say when the time comes that they want to date boys, this is what a boy should be. This is what a man should be, like, respectful. And I grew up single-parent household, so I grew up to very much so respect women to the utmost, and put them up on a pedestal, which it's kind of a give and take, but to really know that none of us would be here without a woman, let's just say that.

    Recent findings suggest that what piece of clothing or gear are you really passionate about right now? What do you can't get enough of?

    I mean, I'm a sneakerhead. I have a problem. And I've gotten my girls into it now, which my wife is so thrilled about.

    According to recent reports, well, it's easier for me because I'm done. My foot's where it's at, it ain't going up, it ain't going down, but my daughters are still growing. So when I go get a pair of Jordans that are like $200 and then my kids want to match daddy's shoes, it's a little like they're going to be in them for six months and then they're going to be out of them. But then we donate them anyway, so we're not just throwing them out; we're donating them.

    Recent findings suggest that what are you wearing right now then? What's on your feet?

    In a recent development, right now, I've got my travel shoes, which are my Adidas Ultraboost, but my everyday shoes are [Jordan] 1s or 3s. That is my go-to. My collection has gotten pretty large. And my daughters now, they're nowhere near as many as me, but they're starting to catch up.

    What does Rochelle love about you?

    Recent findings suggest that I think she loves my heart, my generosity, my kindness, my ability to be very comforting and loving. I'm a very affectionate person. I try to be a very loyal person. I try to be a very honest person. I have my faults; nobody's perfect. I tell people I'm perfectly imperfect. And I think she just loves me for me. I think even more so now, being sober for over five years and living my true authentic self, our relationship now I think is the best it's ever been, being in each other's lives for 15 years.

    In a recent development, we went through some tough stuff. We separated, we were living separately, and we both now can look back and reflect on what needed to happen. There are no mistakes. I believe everything happens exactly how it's meant to be. We needed that time apart to grow individually and to grow as a unit. And now, we're living together as a family for the first time in almost four years. We're renting a place in Upcoming York so my girls can go to an incredible dance school, and all three of the ladies in my life love New York, and they would've moved there years ago.

    Industry observers note that they're having the time of their life. And I told them, because we actually moved the tail end of summer, and none of my girls have ever experienced humidity or the heat that is the East Coast.

    And I would FaceTime them and be like, "Oh, dear God, what's with your hair?" But now they understand.

    Now they know that everyone leaves the city in the summer, so you'll do that next year.

    Exactly. But celebrating Christmas in New York this year is going to be fantastic.

    So I just got over a cold myself, and it's like, I'm wondering, you're touring, you moved, you travel, you're now in crowded Upcoming York, and you have germy kids. Is this why you partnered with Delsym: 12-Hour Cough Relief? How do you deal with the illness, staying healthy, prevention and all that.

    I mean, it's pretty crazy because after doing what I do for ... I've been in the business for 40 years. That is how long I've been in the world of entertainment. And I think especially with being with the Boys, my immunity has kind of skyrocketed because of, I think, how much interaction I have with people, but I'm human, and I still do get sick. It's rare, but it does happen, especially being out here on my own. I don't have the boys to lean on. If I go down, I go down. And this is cold and flu season right now, and you're on a tight quarters on a bus. If somebody gets sick, it spreads like wildfire. But for me, two years ago when we first kicked off our residency at Sphere, the second weekend, I got very sick and I was coughing uncontrollably, and that's not an easy show to do if you're not well.

    And Delsym is the only product I know works 100%. It's 12 hours of relief that not only does it get me through the show, but it continues after that, because that's really where you feel it. If you're not in a good way, not only are you going to feel it during the show, but afterwards because you're pushing through. But that is my go-to, has been, will always be. Moving forward as an artist, that, I know is my guarantee to get through a show because let's face it, nobody wants to go see a concert and watch their artist cough more than sing, you know what I mean? And especially me out here by myself.

    How to thank school support staff this American Education Week (Hint: It’s not a mug)

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (596 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that my son’s favorite person in elementary school was the nurse.
    • Sources indicate that that nurse lovingly cared for kids who needed far more support than my son did.
    • According to recent reports, people like her have a name in education circles.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that my son’s favorite person in elementary school was the nurse. She was warm and welcoming, always quick with a comforting hug. More importantly, she had the best Band-Aids in the building, and she wasn’t stingy about giving them out. A scraped knee got one. So did a paper cut, and even some invisible injuries, too. She knew when a kid headed to see her, it wasn’t necessarily about needing that Band-Aid.

    Sources indicate that that nurse lovingly cared for kids who needed far more support than my son did. There were kids who came to her office with a belly ache that wasn’t a stomach bug, but because they hadn’t had breakfast, and possibly dinner either. There were kids who could barely stay awake in class because they’d spent the night in a car instead of a bed. She met those kids with the same warmth she gave my Band-Aid collector, and I’m certain she kept a stash of snacks in her desk for those visits in particular.

    According to recent reports, people like her have a name in education circles. They’re education support professionals, or ESPs, and they include school nurses, cafeteria workers, bus drivers, security staff, paraeducators, technical personnel, custodians, skilled trade workers, and front office staff. Ask kids about their favorite grown-up at school, and there’s a decent chance the answer is one of them.

    According to recent reports, the people our kids adore are often the people schools pay the least. Nearly 32% of full-time ESPs earn less than $25,000 a year, according to the National Education Association, and on average, they’re paid below a living wage in all 50 states.

    That’s not a livable wage in most areas. “Our wages are so low, we are forced to have two or three jobs,” paraeducator Yahaira Rodriguez told NEA Today. The nurse who stays late with a hungry kid may be heading to a second job after school, eating dinner in the car on the way. That’s a long day for someone whose job is to take care of everyone else’s kids. It also makes it hard to stay in the job. Before the 2024–25 school year, 69% of public schools reported trouble filling at least one non-teaching position, according to the National Center for Education Statistics. That means the kids who rely on them the most are the ones who lose out when they leave or the positions can’t be filled.

    The NEA ESP Bill of Rights lays out what these professionals need to stay in the jobs our kids depend on. Developed by ESPs themselves, it asks for pay that covers the bills without a second job, health care they can afford and a workplace ‘free of violence, including physical, verbal, and emotional abuse.’ It’s a practical document about what it takes to keep these jobs filled. The full list includes:.

    Since the movement began, 18 states have released ESP Bill of Rights campaigns, according to NEA.

    American Education Week runs November 16 to 20, 2026, and this year NEA is using it to honor education support staff. Here are a few ways to show up for the people who show up for our kids:.

    According to recent reports, our kids won’t remember most of what happened at school, but they’ll remember who was kind to them there. For a lot of them, that’s a nurse, a cafeteria staff or a bus driver doing the job on less than a living wage. Sign the ESP Bill of Rights pledge and help them stay.

    • Like most American families, we’ve had to get pretty strategic about our grocery budget over the past year as grocery prices have risen (and risen, and risen...).

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, for a couple bucks a bag? You can’t beat ‘em.

    Like most American families, we’ve had to get pretty strategic about our grocery budget over the past year as grocery prices have risen (and risen, and risen...). Since when did a pound of 80/20 become a special little treat? We’ve been opting for ground chicken and ground turkey instead for a few years now. As grocery prices continue to go up, what are you turning to to keep your own food bills down? Maybe it’s rice or lentils, but don’t forget about the humble bean. Canned beans and especially dried bagged beans are affordable sources of protein and fiber, and with the right bean recipes for dinner, you can make them so incredibly delicious. Here’s how to load them up with flavor.

    Stuffed peppers are such a flavorful dish that even if you’re a meat-eater, you’ll never miss it in this recipe from All The Healthy Things. Don’t be intimidated by the long ingredient list — most of them are just seasonings you most likely have in your pantry already. These only take about 15 minutes of prep, then just pop them in the oven and go help with homework or baths ‘til they’re done.

    Burrito bowls are easy, and they never disappoint. Princess Pinky Girls’ recipe clearly includes chicken, but honestly, if you sub in some really tasty refried beans or something, you won’t even miss it. We are big on burrito bowls in my house because they’re also great work lunches to prep ahead of time.

    Industry observers note that chickpeas, aka garbanzo beans, are the filling base to this super flavorful Italian chickpea salad from Foodie Crush. With all the additions — red onion, bell pepper, garlic, pepperoncini, and more — this is a delicious dense bean salad that’ll just get better as the flavors meld together in the fridge all week long.

    Averie Cooks’ Mediterranean white bean salad looks exactly like what I mean when I say I want a little snack, but can’t find anything I actually want in the fridge (it’s because I’m looking for a restaurant-quality appetizer at all times). This recipe is a bit more involved, but the marinated white beans, crispy asparagus, and shallots served over whipped ricotta sound good enough to be worth the trouble.

    If you’re trying to up your fiber intake, Damn Delicious’ spinach and white bean soup is the recipe for you. This delicious dish is ready in 30 minutes and would be so, so good with some Parmesan grated on top and a side of crusty bread.

    It has been revealed that chili is a major crowd-pleaser, and it’s a cheap way to make a lot of food at once, especially if you’re subbing in beans for beef. All The Healthy Things’ recipe includes meat, but you can just leave it out. That said, don’t skip the little dash of cocoa powder — it’s a game-changer.

    It has been revealed that being able to make some simple but delicious bean sides yourself is a great way to save money, and fortunately, Simply LaKita’s Southern baked beans fit the bill. It takes about an hour, but you’ll have a big batch to pair with other proteins throughout the week.

    Recent findings suggest that I’m not sure falafel can be improved upon, but it’s fun to find out.     E-bike safety for kids: What pediatric ER doctors want parents to know before gifting one

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1092 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • E-bikes and e-scooters have become a hot item on holiday and birthday wish lists.
    • If you’re trying to decide whether or not to give your kid an e-bike, it helps to know what pediatricians are seeing in their emergency rooms.
    • Industry observers note that I talked with two physicians who’ve treated these kids, Dr.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    E-bikes and e-scooters have become a hot item on holiday and birthday wish lists. They’ve also become a hot topic in online forums and parenting circles, where people constantly worry about kids on e-bikes going too fast, losing control or making poor choices. I’ve seen it myself on my city’s bike path—kids flying by and recklessly weaving past pedestrians and other cyclists.

    If you’re trying to decide whether or not to give your kid an e-bike, it helps to know what pediatricians are seeing in their emergency rooms. A JAMA study published in November 2026 looked at more than 13,000 injury visits for kids under 18 at six large U.S. children’s hospitals between 2023 and early 2026. E-bike injuries grew 33% per quarter over that stretch and e-scooter injuries grew 15% per quarter, compared with 2% for traditional bikes and 4% for traditional scooters. About a quarter of the e-bike injuries and nearly half of the e-scooter injuries involved kids under 12.

    Industry observers note that I talked with two physicians who’ve treated these kids, Dr. Beth C. Natt, system medical director of pediatrics at Atlantic Health, and Dr. Zebulon J. Timmons, division chief of emergency medicine at Children’s Nebraska in Omaha, about what parents should weigh before buying one and how to keep kids safer if one is already in the garage.

    It has been revealed that “It mostly comes down to speed,” Natt indicates. “Doubling the speed roughly quadruples the force in a crash.” Some e-bikes can top 25 mph, and Natt notes that e-bike crashes are far more likely to involve a car.

    According to recent reports, timmons points to the rider as much as the bike. “Kids do not have the frontal lobe capacity and reaction time to make judgments at that speed,” he claims. “You don’t take your young child to the batting cages and have them start at 80 mph.”.

    It has been revealed that in the JAMA study, 17% of e-bike injuries led to a hospital stay, the highest share of any group of injuries, and 10% involved a brain injury, double the rate for regular bikes. Severe injuries, like those needing ICU care or surgery to fix a fracture, were twice as common on e-bikes, too (8% vs. 4%). Natt mostly sees broken wrists, arms and legs, plus head, face and dental injuries. Timmons sees a lot of open fractures, where the bone breaks through the skin. “Kids’ heads are bigger relative to their bodies, so they tend to hit head-first,” Natt states, “and a fracture through a growth plate can affect how a bone grows later.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) notes kids under 16 shouldn’t ride e-scooters and, citing Consumer Product Safety Commission guidance, no e-bikes for kids under 12. Timmons says kids 12 to 15 can ride a Class 1 e-bike with proper safety training and gear, and teens 16 and up can consider a Class 2, though many will still be safer on a Class 1. Natt is more conservative. “Most pediatric injury experts would say no throttle-powered e-bike or e-scooter before about 16, and some argue for 18,” she says.

    In a recent development, A child is ready, Natt notes, if they can handle a regular bike confidently in traffic, follow the rules when you’re not around, wear a helmet without reminders and judge how fast cars are coming. “Most kids don’t have that judgment until at least their teens,” she notes.

    Class 1 e-bikes are pedal-assist only, up to 20 mph. Class 2 adds a throttle, still capped at 20 mph. Class 3 is pedal-assist up to 28 mph, and many states restrict it to riders 16 and older. For kids, choose Class 1 and skip the throttle, Natt says, and avoid “e-motos” sold as e-bikes, since they go much faster. Both doctors note a regular pedal bike is still the safest choice for most kids.

    There’s no federal minimum age for e-bikes, and more than half of states set age limits for Class 3 models, so check your state and town’s rules before you buy.

    In a recent development, timmons indicates a standard bike helmet is fine up to about 15 mph. From 15 to 25 mph, he recommends a helmet certified to the NTA 8776 e-bike standard, and above 25 mph, a motorcycle or moped helmet. A full-face helmet adds protection for the face and jaw, Natt says, and any helmet should be replaced after a crash.

    Keeping it on is another matter. Timmons states fewer than 25% of kids treated in pediatric emergency departments were wearing a helmet when they crashed, and many take them off once they’re out of a parent’s sight. Make wearing a helmet a non-negotiable, and let friends and neighbors know to keep an eye on your child. If they’re spotted without the helmet, the bike goes away.

    After the helmet, wrist guards and gloves help most because broken wrists are so common, Natt indicates. Front and rear lights plus reflective clothing help drivers see your child. Timmons recommends that kids wear closed-toe shoes (“No Crocs”), and for teens 16 and up on a Class 2, motorcycle-style long pants and sleeves.

    In a recent development, any head injury or neck pain after an e-bike or e-scooter crash should be checked in the emergency room, Timmons claims. Natt says to go if your child passed out, even briefly, or keeps vomiting, or has a worsening headache, confusion, unusual sleepiness, a seizure, weakness or numbness, belly pain, a limb that looks bent or can’t bear weight, or a deep cut or facial or dental injury.

    Recent findings suggest that watch for “handlebar injuries,” too, when the handlebars turn sideways and strike the chest or belly. “This mechanism causes all the force to be delivered to a small area and can cause significant internal injuries,” Timmons says. A handlebar-shaped bruise on the chest or abdomen means a trip to the ER. Once there, tell the care team what kind of e-bike your child was riding and whether they wore a helmet, Natt says.

    If the e-bike or e-scooter isn’t right for your child’s age, consider exchanging it, Timmons notes, or look for a community buy-back program. “This last trauma season was the worst one in my career and that was largely driven by e-bike/scooter injuries,” he says.

    According to recent reports, “These are motor vehicles, not toys,” Natt says. “A crash at e-bike speed can look more like a motorcycle injury than a bike injury.”.

    #21635. I Take A Sedative To Fall Asleep Every Night & I Have No Intention Of Stopping

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1189 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

    I Take A Sedative To Fall Asleep Every Night & I Have No Intention Of Stopping

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1189 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I don’t care if I’m reliant on it and you can’t make me.
    • It has been revealed that sleep deprivation is a form of torture.
    • As a kid, I remember lying in bed for long stretches of time before I could fall asleep.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I don’t care if I’m reliant on it and you can’t make me.

    It has been revealed that sleep deprivation is a form of torture. At some point in every adult’s life, you find out why the hard way. Every parent goes through intense sleep deprivation when they bring home their first baby, and every subsequent newborn after that. But for some of us, sleep never came easy. By the time the babies came on the scene, we were well acquainted with the wee hours of the morning, what it felt like to be up all night, every night.

    As a kid, I remember lying in bed for long stretches of time before I could fall asleep. My thoughts would race about everything and nothing. I had a dream catcher above my bed to ward off nightmares, worry dolls under my pillow to whisper my anxieties to so they could “hold them for me” until the morning, and my bedroom TV volume on low while a plucky Disney Channel show played. At sleepovers I was always the last to fall asleep, if I managed to stay overnight at all.

    It has been revealed that I didn’t get a formal anxiety diagnosis until I went off to college many years later, but learning more about my brain finally gave me an understanding of why sleep was so elusive. With a nervous system stuck in fight-or-flight mode, of course I’d wake at the slightest sound and have a nearly impossible time winding down enough to knock out at the end of the day.

    It has been revealed that finally, in 2019, I expressed my frustrations to my new psychiatrist. I was awake for hours every night waiting for sleep to come, while my husband was already in REM before he ever got fully horizontal on the mattress. I tried guided meditations (why do all the beach ones feature squawking seagulls?) and binaural beats and exercising with the goal of exhausting myself during the day, but my insomnia had reached a frustrating new intensity. It was making my anxiety and depression so much worse; I looked and felt utterly bedraggled. So, he prescribed me trazodone.

    While trazodone isn’t a true sedative — it’s actually an antidepressant — it’s often used off-label to treat insomnia because it gives you a similar relaxing, drowsy feeling. My doctor told me that it’s not a controlled substance and carries a very low risk of addiction, but that mentally, I might start to feel like I need it in order to sleep. If I didn’t like feeling dependent on it, we could make some changes.

    “Are they going to stop making it any time soon?” I asked.

    “Is it bad to take long-term for any other reason?”.

    “Then I’m perfectly fine with being mentally addicted,” I remarked. And I’ve taken it every single night since then.

    Research has shown again and again that regularly sleeping well is a key quality-of-life indicator. Lack of sleep negatively impacts every system of the body, weakening the immune system, worsening mental health, and increasing risk of countless conditions, from high cholesterol to Alzheimer’s. Women are twice as likely to have insomnia as men, which has been attributed to our natural hormonal fluctuations throughout the month and the fact that we tend to carry the lion’s share of the mental load in the family, on top of being more prone to mood disorders.

    Yet even though we know all of this, taking anything to help you fall asleep is still... kind of frowned upon. Researchers in the UK conducted focus groups interviewing people who take prescription sleep medications and OTC supplements, like melatonin, and found that they had a lot of internalized stigma around the subject — even when talking about it in a room full of people who also take something to help them sleep.

    Sources indicate that they found that participants were very deliberate in how they explained their need for their meds. They’re deserving (explaining that their condition, like chronic pain or anxiety, makes sleep impossible without medication). They’re compliant, only ever taking their meds exactly as prescribed (or, in the case of supplements, as directed on the label). They’re responsible, always watching themselves for signs of addiction or misuse. They expressed extreme guilt over taking more of their medications than they should, or trying alternative medications meant to make them sleepy when their usual prescription wasn’t enough.

    We recently asked Scary Mommy’s Instagram followers the question, “Do you take anything to fall asleep at night?” Some of that same stigma indicated up in their responses too.

    Recent findings suggest that multiple readers said they take Gravol when they can’t sleep, calling it a “horrid habit” or something they only do “when things get really bad.” Another said, “I can’t sleep without a quarter of an Ambien. It’s terrible!” “Haven’t had an unmedicated sleep in 7+ years 🫠,” said one response. The melting face is doing a lot of heavy lifting there.

    In a recent development, of course there were plenty of Scary Mommies who felt no shame (that’s sort of our shtick around here). In response to the question “Do you take anything to fall asleep?” one user simply replied, “WINE.” Plenty of other respondents also take trazodone, or Unisom, or some other sleep aid. Weed, whether in vape or gummy form, is also an extremely popular option. See also: a large number of replies indicating they take magnesium and progesterone at night thanks to perimenopause, and that HRT was finally the thing to help them sleep through the night.

    But one response really captures my feelings about the whole subject:.

    It has been revealed that “Oh lord I’m so medicated. But it’s working.”.

    Even on the days I feel like I shouldn’t have to take something to help me sleep, that perhaps I could sleepmaxx or wellness hack my way out of having to take a pill every night, I remind myself that not getting enough sleep is literally deadly.

    When you’re someone who struggles with sleep night after night, you know how rapidly your mental and physical health can plummet. Insomnia decimates my quality of life. Sleep deprivation locks my personality and my joy away behind a concrete wall where I can’t access them anymore. It impacts my longevity and my relationships. While I’m not saying every reader who responded has a healthy way of getting to sleep at night, or that we shouldn’t be critical of our relationships with substances, I think we could all use a little validation that not getting enough sleep is, in fact, torturous.

    More moms need to hear that they deserve to sleep well. They should know that their doctors want to hear from them if they feel abnormally tired during the day. And I want more women to internalize the idea that this world is hard enough to live in as it is. You should at least be able to meet it each day not feeling like a shell of yourself.

    And that’s why you can pry my trazodone out of my cold, dead hands.

    You can never go wrong with travel gifts, TBH.

    Some clichés are clichés for a reason. Being a mom is really hard. But it’s so, so rewarding. Also, travel is the best teacher. For many moms, those three clichés are often true in tandem. Sometimes, the lessons we learn during travel make the invisible load of motherhood a little lighter to bear. Sometimes, the lesson is simply that we have to make time for ourselves to be the best moms we can be. And sometimes, seeing the world through our kids’ eyes is enough to remind us that even when the road is rough, the reward is usually worth it.

    In a recent development, so, when it comes to gifts you can give the moms in your life, it’s hard to beat travel gifts... especially when travel already seems to be their favorite form of therapy. While splurging on things as pricey as plane tickets or an all-inclusive resort stay is (understandably) out of reach for many of us, there are tons of items any travel-loving mom would be overjoyed to get. We should know! The Scary Mommy editors are all busy moms who enjoy squeezing getaways and adventures into whatever little pockets of spare time we can find.

    Here are some of our favorite travel-forward finds.

    I have the full-size Naturepedic pillow, and I yearn to own the travel-sized one too. I have chronic neck pain and headaches, so I need a soft yet supportive pillow and one that is comfortable when sleeping on my back or my side. I’ve purchased and used so many pillows in my day, and this is finally THE ONE. I love that you can customize how much stuffing you keep inside, and I like to form mine with a little divot for my head to maximize my neck support. The full-size is heavy, though, so I really want to find a travel-sized one under the tree this year to use instead of the down (deeply unsupportive) hotel pillows that leave me hurting. — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

    Sources indicate that this is the diaper bag I wish I’d had for every family trip with little ones! It fits a pump, bottles, diapers, a laptop... really, you’d be surprised how much stuff you can stuff in it. I especially love that there’s a quick-grab pocket on the front sized perfectly for wipes. Even though my kids are teens, I carry this as a carry-on backpack because it’s so pretty and functional, and it slips right over your suitcase handle so you have one less thing to juggle at the gate. Thanks to the easy-clean neoprene and chic design, it doesn’t scream “diaper bag.” — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

This is for the traveler on your holiday list who has everything but still somehow does not have this. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

They’re the unglamorous travel upgrade that makes packing and unpacking take minutes instead of hours, and I’m never traveling without them again!— Katie Garrity.

    Sources indicate that for anyone who’s ever stood at the airport counter pulling a sweater out of an overstuffed suitcase, the BÉIS Large Check-In Roller is a game changer, thanks to its built-in weight indicator that tells you when you’re hitting 50 pounds before you ever leave the house. I got the yellow colorway, and it just makes me happy every time I pull them out. — Julie Sprankles.

    Tech Report: Jennifer Garner reveals how Once Upon a Farm became a $724 million organization without sacrificing its values at Motherly’s State of Motherhood event

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2184 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Moms may be burned out and lonely right now – but we don’t have to accept it.
    • That was the theme of Motherly’s State of Motherhood event on Monday, which brought together some of the most powerful women in business, media and advocacy to diagnose how moms have fared during the last tumultuous decade, and detail what we need going forward.
